name: Query Rewriting and HyDE
question: Can a model turn the question into a better search?
summary: Uses an LLM before retrieval to make the question searchable. It rewrites a chatty follow-up into a standalone query using the conversation, generates a few alternative phrasings and fuses their results (multi-query), splits a multi-part question into sub-queries, or writes a hypothetical answer and embeds that instead of the question (HyDE). Each trick raises recall at the cost of an LLM call. Ordering the results afterwards is a separate step: re-ranking.
useCases: Conversational follow-ups such as “and the other one?”
Documents that use different words from the users
Multi-part questions that need several searches

items.detail: turn chatty or vague input into a standalone search query
search several phrasings and merge with reciprocal rank fusion
embed a hypothetical answer instead of the question
split a complex question into sub-queries
search a more general question alongside the specific one

steps: Rewrite follow-ups into standalone queries using the chat history
Add multi-query with fusion when documents use varied wording
Try HyDE for short or vague questions and compare with the plain query
Measure recall and latency before and after each addition
pitfalls: Every LLM step adds latency and cost
Rewrites can drift from what the user meant
HyDE can invent details that pull retrieval off course
remember: Fix the question before you search.
caption: Rewriting puts the right passage in the pool; re-ranking then moves it up.

steps.title: Rewrite the follow-up
steps.text: “and what about the other one?” has nothing to search on. An LLM uses the chat history to write a standalone query.

steps.title: Generate alternative phrasings
steps.text: Multi-query asks for a few rephrasings, because documents may use different words: exit load, redemption charge, exit fee.

steps.title: Retrieve wide and merge
steps.text: Run hybrid search for every phrasing, merge the lists with reciprocal rank fusion and keep 50 candidates. The right passage is in the pool, at rank 23.

steps.title: Re-rank with a cross-encoder
steps.text: A cross-encoder reads the query and each passage together, which is more accurate than comparing two vectors. The right passage moves from 23 to 2.

steps.title: Send only the top 5 to the model
steps.text: Only the best few passages go into the prompt, so the model sees the right one without a pile of noise.

steps.title: Measure what each step buys
steps.text: Compare recall@5 and latency with and without each step. Here recall@5 rises from 0.62 to 0.88 for about 410 ms more per query.

library.name: sentence-transformers CrossEncoder
library.what: Open-source re-rankers that read the query and passage together. Cohere Rerank is the common hosted alternative.

samples.code:
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder

history  = "User asked about the exit load on the Flexi Cap Fund."
followup = "and what about the other one, the balanced fund?"

query = llm(f"Rewrite as a standalone search query.\n"
            f"Context: {history}\nQuestion: {followup}")
# -> "exit load Balanced Advantage Fund"

candidates = hybrid_search(query, k=50)              # wide recall first
reranker = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2")
scores = reranker.predict([(query, c) for c in candidates])
top5 = [c for _, c in sorted(zip(scores, candidates), reverse=True)[:5]]

numericDrill.question: Retrieval returns 50 candidates and the right passage is at rank 23. Your prompt uses the top 5. After re-ranking it moves to rank 2. What happens to recall@5 for this query?
numericDrill.answer: It goes from 0 (rank 23 is outside the top 5) to 1. The retriever had found it; the ranking was the problem, which is exactly what re-ranking fixes.

interview.question: What is HyDE, and when does it help?
interview.answer: Hypothetical Document Embeddings: an LLM writes a plausible answer and you embed that instead of the question. It helps when questions are short or phrased very differently from the documents, and can hurt if the hypothetical answer invents false details.

interview.question: Where does a re-ranker go in the pipeline?
interview.answer: After a wide, cheap retrieval step (hybrid top 50–100) and before building the prompt. It improves precision at the very top, which is what the model sees.

mistakes.mistake: Re-ranking only the top 5 you already had

mistakes.fix: Rewrite vague or conversational queries; skip clear ones to save latency

quiz.question: Mid-chat, “what about the second one?” retrieves unrelated documents. What is the fix?
options: Rewrite the query with an LLM using the chat history
quiz.explanation: The query alone has nothing to search on. A standalone rewrite restores the missing context.

quiz.question: Where does a cross-encoder re-ranker belong in a product-search pipeline?
options: Before retrieval, to pick the index
After a wide first-stage retrieval, before building the results
Instead of retrieval, over the full catalogue
After the LLM writes its answer
quiz.explanation: Retrieve many cheap candidates, then re-rank a short list precisely.

quiz.question: Which statements about HyDE are true? Select all that apply.
options: It embeds a hypothetical answer instead of the question
It can help when questions are short or phrased unlike the documents
It can bias retrieval if the hypothetical answer invents details
It removes the need for a retriever
quiz.explanation: HyDE changes what is embedded; retrieval still happens, and invented details are its main risk.

quiz.question: The right passage is at rank 23 of 50 candidates and the prompt uses the top 5. Re-ranking moves it to rank 2. What happens to recall@5 for this query?
quiz.explanation: Rank 23 is outside the top 5; rank 2 is inside. The retriever found it; re-ranking fixed the order.

quiz.question: Search takes 40 ms, the rewrite call 350 ms, and re-ranking costs 20 ms plus 2 ms per candidate. What is the latency with 50 candidates?
“Compare roaming charges in the UAE and the UK” retrieves only UAE documents. What helps most?
options: Decompose it into one sub-query per country
quiz.explanation: Multi-part questions need several searches whose results are merged.

quiz.question: Why not run a cross-encoder over all 5 million passages for every query?
options: Cross-encoders are less accurate than bi-encoders
Nothing can be precomputed, so each query needs 5 million forward passes
They only accept one passage per day
quiz.explanation: A cross-encoder reads each query–passage pair together, so the cost grows with the corpus for every query.

quiz.question: What are the risks of adding LLM query rewriting? Select all that apply.
options: The rewrite can drift from what the user meant
It guarantees answers free of hallucination
quiz.explanation: Rewriting helps recall but costs time and money and can change the meaning. It guarantees nothing about answers.

quiz.question: Multi-query search runs four phrasings and returns four ranked lists. How are they usually merged?
quiz.explanation: RRF combines rankings robustly without comparing raw scores.

quiz.question: A rewrite call costs ₹0.02 per query and the site serves 3 lakh queries a day. What is the daily cost?
Before indexing, an LLM writes a one-sentence note on where each chunk sits in its document, and the note is embedded with the chunk. What is this called?
quiz.explanation: Anthropic’s contextual retrieval prepends chunk-specific context before embedding and BM25 indexing.

quiz.question: A pipeline retrieves 5 candidates, re-ranks them and keeps the top 5. Recall did not improve. Why?
options: Re-ranking can only reorder the same 5 passages; retrieve wider first
The top 5 should be the top 3
quiz.explanation: To improve recall at 5, the first stage must surface the right passage somewhere in a larger pool.

quiz.question: When is it reasonable to skip LLM query rewriting? Select all that apply.
options: The query is a precise policy number
The latency budget is tight and the query is already clear
The query is a clear, complete question
The query is a follow-up full of pronouns
quiz.explanation: Rewrite where it pays: vague and follow-up questions. Clear queries can skip it to save latency.

quiz.question: Your budget is 600 ms. Rewrite plus re-ranking takes 520 ms, and multi-query would add 420 ms. What do you do?
options: Keep rewrite and re-ranking; skip multi-query or trigger it only for hard queries
quiz.explanation: 940 ms breaks the budget. Add expensive steps only where they are measured to pay off.

quiz.question: What should you log to evaluate query rewriting in production? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Comparing original, rewrite and retrieved results shows drift and recall problems. The answer alone hides them.

quiz.question: First-stage recall@50 is 0.92. Even with a perfect re-ranker, what is the highest recall@5 you can reach?
quiz.explanation: A re-ranker cannot surface passages outside the 50 candidates.

quiz.question: Which of these act before retrieval runs? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Rewriting, HyDE and decomposition shape the search; re-ranking works on its results.

quiz.question: With HyDE, the hypothetical answer mentions the wrong dosage, and retrieval returns a page about a different drug. What went wrong?
options: The hypothetical answer invented details that steered retrieval
quiz.explanation: HyDE’s main risk: invented details bias which documents look similar.

quiz.question: You need multilingual re-ranking in production with no GPUs to manage. Which tool fits?
quiz.explanation: A hosted re-ranking API avoids running models yourself.

quiz.question: What does a cross-encoder take as input and return?
options: A query–passage pair; a relevance score
quiz.explanation: It scores pairs directly instead of producing vectors to compare.
